title: Department of Commerce v. New York (2019)
shortTitle: Department of Commerce v. New York (2019)
summary: An agency decision that is otherwise reasonable and reasonably explained must still be set aside and remanded when the record shows that the sole stated reason for it was contrived and did not reflect the agency's actual decisionmaking.
notes:
Key line: "Accepting contrived reasons would defeat the purpose of the enterprise." (Roberts, C.J.)

Citation: 588 U.S. 752 (2019).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were the Department of Commerce, Secretary of Commerce Wilbur Ross, the Census Bureau and its officials. The respondents were two groups of plaintiffs whose suits were consolidated: New York and seventeen other states, the District of Columbia, fifteen cities and counties, and the United States Conference of Mayors; and non governmental organizations led by the New York Immigration Coalition. The Department of Justice, which had sent the December 2017 letter requesting citizenship data, was not a party but its role was central to the pretext question. The case reached the Court on certiorari before judgment to the Second Circuit.
sections.Material Facts: The Census Act delegates to the Secretary the task of conducting the decennial census in such form and content as he may determine. Secretary Ross took office in February 2017 and within about a week began taking steps to reinstate a citizenship question. His Director of Policy, who did not know why, saw his task as finding the best rationale and unsuccessfully solicited requests for citizenship data from the Department of Homeland Security and DOJ's Executive Office for Immigration Review. After Ross contacted the Attorney General directly, DOJ's Civil Rights Division sent a letter dated December 12, 2017, drafted with heavy input from Commerce staff, asking for block level citizenship data to enforce the Voting Rights Act, and then declined the Census Bureau's offer to discuss alternatives. On March 26, 2018, Ross issued a memo reinstating the question, citing only the DOJ request and rejecting the Bureau's advice that administrative records would produce better data.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York alleging violations of the Enumeration Clause, the APA and equal protection. After the government filed the administrative record and a supplemental memo disclosing that Ross had considered the question since early 2017, the court ordered completion of the record and authorized extra record discovery, including a deposition of the Secretary that the Supreme Court stayed. Following a bench trial, the court found standing and held that the decision was arbitrary and capricious, rested on a pretextual rationale and violated sections 6(c) and 141(f) of the Census Act, 351 F. Supp. 3d 502 (2019), but rejected the equal protection claim. The Supreme Court granted certiorari before judgment, heard argument on April 23, 2019, and on June 27, 2019, affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded.
sections.Issue: Whether the state respondents had standing; whether the Enumeration Clause permits a citizenship question; whether the Secretary's decision was reviewable under the APA or committed to agency discretion by law; whether the decision was arbitrary and capricious or violated sections 6(c) and 141(f) of the Census Act; and whether the district court properly set the decision aside on the ground that the Secretary's stated rationale, improving Voting Rights Act enforcement at DOJ's request, was pretextual, including whether the court could consider evidence outside the administrative record in reaching that conclusion.
sections.Holding: The Court held that several states had standing because an undercount of noncitizen households would cost them federal funds; that the Enumeration Clause permits asking about citizenship, given Congress's broad authority and long historical practice; that the decision was reviewable because the Census Act supplies meaningful standards; and that the Secretary's choice to reinstate the question and supplement it with administrative records was reasonable and reasonably explained and did not violate sections 6(c) or 141(f). But the Court, by a 5 to 4 vote in Part V, held that the district court was warranted in remanding to the agency because the evidence showed a significant mismatch between the decision and the rationale provided: the VRA rationale, the sole stated reason, seemed to have been contrived.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts set out settled propositions: an agency must disclose the basis of its action; a court is ordinarily limited to the contemporaneous explanation and the administrative record under Vermont Yankee and Camp v. Pitts; a court may not reject stated reasons merely because the agency also had unstated ones, including political considerations; but under Overton Park a strong showing of bad faith or improper behavior justifies inquiry into the decisionmakers' mental processes and extra record discovery. The district court's extra record discovery order was premature, but the more than 12,000 pages of deliberative materials later added to the record largely justified it, so the Court reviewed the pretext ruling on all the evidence. It is not improper for an agency head to arrive with policy preferences, sound out other agencies and have staff substantiate a legal basis, and no single step was defective. Yet the record showed that the Secretary was determined to reinstate the question from the start, that no one considered the VRA until late, that Commerce went to great lengths to elicit a request from any willing agency, and that DOJ's interest was directed more to helping Commerce than to obtaining data. Unlike a case with both stated and unstated reasons, the sole stated reason did not match the record. The reasoned explanation requirement exists so that agencies offer genuine justifications that courts and the public can scrutinize.

topics.lrs-n-administrative-record: An exceptional expanded record revealed that the sole stated census rationale was contrived.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The five-Justice majority applied deferential arbitrary-and-capricious review to uphold the Secretary's policy choice on the record before rejecting the pretextual rationale.
topics.lrs-o-chenery-reasons: The pretext holding rests on the Chenery principle that agency action must be sustained, if at all, on the reasons the agency actually gave, and it shows when a court may look behind the stated rationale.
topics.lrs-n-standing-state: The Court found that the state plaintiffs had Article III standing on the basis of a predicted census undercount causing loss of federal funds.

learning.separateOpinions: Parts I and II were unanimous; Parts III, IV-B and IV-C were joined by Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch and Kavanaugh; Part IV-A by Justices Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor, Kagan and Kavanaugh; and Part V by Justices Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan. Justice Thomas, joined by Justices Gorsuch and Kavanaugh, dissented from Part V, arguing that the Court for the first time invalidated agency action solely by questioning the sincerity of an otherwise adequate rationale, disregarded the presumption of regularity, and invited endless discovery into agency motives. Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Ginsburg, Sotomayor and Kagan, agreed on pretext but would also have held the decision arbitrary and capricious because the Secretary ignored the Bureau's evidence that the question would reduce accuracy. Justice Alito would have held the decision committed to agency discretion by law and unreviewable under the APA.
